meta.title: Vietnamese B1 Intermediate
meta.subtitle: 1000 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Vietnamese → English (see the Vietnamese, recall the meaning) and English → Vietnamese (see an English meaning, recall the Vietnamese). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1000 words for an intermediate learner, aligned to B1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand the main points of clear standard input on familiar matters regularly encountered in work, school, leisure, etc.' — a learner here is able to deal with most situations likely to arise while travelling, to produce simple connected text on familiar topics, and to describe experiences and events, dreams, hopes and ambitions, and briefly give reasons and explanations for opinions and plans. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: Vietnam's own framework for learners of Vietnamese publishes no graded word list, and neither does any exam board, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 220 of the 1000 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — work and careers, money and the economy, education, the news, media and technology, government, law and society, the environment and nature, health and medicine, travel and transport, the household and its chores, relationships and the stages of life, feelings and character, religion, customs and festivals, abstract nouns for ideas, reasons and plans, the connectors that join sentences, and the verbs of thinking, deciding, arguing and changing — and the other 780 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Vietnamese, counted in film and television subtitles. Vietnamese writes a space between syllables rather than between words, so the subtitles were divided into words against the dictionary first, and a two-syllable word such as học sinh (pupil) is counted as one word. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Beneath every headword its tones are named, one per syllable — ngang (no mark), huyền (à), sắc (á), hỏi (ả), ngã (ã) and nặng (ạ) — read off the marks the word is spelt with. 90 nouns show their classifier, the word that stands between a number and the noun (hai con mèo, two cats), and 448 words borrowed from Chinese show the characters they come from. The pronunciation is given in IPA for Hanoi and, where it differs, for Saigon. Real example sentences come with 929 of the 1000 words, three apiece for 771 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Spellings are Wiktionary's, which often puts the tone mark in the older place (hoà, khoẻ); the newer (hòa, khỏe) is equally correct. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, classifiers, characters and pronunciation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: the OpenSubtitles 2018 Vietnamese text (opensubtitles.org, via the OPUS corpus collection), counted here. Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
